opus-5.5.text:
I think those are really different questions, and people tend to blur them together.

On manufacturing, biology is extraordinarily impressive. A cell builds itself out of cheap inputs, with atomically precise machinery, at a rate that human factories can't touch if you measure "how quickly does this system make a copy of itself." A bacterium doubles in maybe twenty minutes. Algae or duckweed can double in a day or two. The most self-replicating human industrial systems take something like a year or more if you ask how long the whole economy would take to build a second copy of its capital stock. So on the "how fast can you build more of the thing" axis, biology is far ahead, and that's a big part of why I take seriously the idea that advanced technology could eventually support very fast growth.

Operating performance is a separate question: once you've built the thing, how well does it do the job and what does it cost to run? There, the picture is much more mixed. Human-made systems often win clearly. Solar panels convert sunlight to usable energy more efficiently than photosynthesis. Motors and engines put out far more power per kilogram than muscle for many tasks. Computers do serial arithmetic billions of times faster than neurons. Biology is stuck with constraints like operating at body temperature, in water, with materials that have to self-assemble, and with designs that evolution could reach incrementally. Engineers aren't bound by those constraints.

Brains are an interesting middle case. On energy efficiency per operation the brain still looks very good compared to current hardware, but that's partly about the computing paradigm, and it's not obvious it's a fundamental limit.

So the way I'd frame it: biology mostly gives us an existence proof about what's possible in manufacturing and self-replication, which is the thing human industry is worst at relative to the frontier. It doesn't tell us that biological designs are the ceiling on performance, and in many domains we've already surpassed them. The interesting forecasting question is what happens when you combine the two: machines with engineered performance plus manufacturing approaching biological doubling times. That's where you'd get growth rates that look very different from anything in history.

r001.rationale: It says biology is much faster at self-replication using cheap inputs, but gives no estimate of a five-to-six-orders-of-magnitude manufacturing energy-cost advantage.

r002.rationale: It describes mixed operating-cost and performance comparisons, with examples where human-made systems excel, but gives no tentative estimate of a roughly three-orders-of-magnitude advantage excluding manufacturing costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd carve it up is something like this. When you look at biological systems, there are a few distinct things going on that are easy to run together.

One is that biology is just incredibly good at manufacturing. A cell can replicate itself in something like an hour under good conditions, using a pretty cheap feedstock, at room temperature, with molecular precision. If you tried to build a factory that takes in sugar and some salts and spits out a copy of itself, humans are not anywhere close to being able to do that. The whole industrial base for making a modern chip is something like trillions of dollars of capital, and it doesn't self-replicate at all. So that's one axis: how fast and how cheaply can you make more of the thing.

A second axis is how cheap it is to run the thing once you've made it. The classic example people point to is the brain: it's doing something impressive on maybe twenty watts, whereas the compute we'd need to run a comparably capable model is drawing orders of magnitude more power. That's an operating-cost advantage, and it's a different fact from the manufacturing one. You could imagine a world where biology was cheap to build but expensive to run, or vice versa.

And then the third thing is performance in the narrow sense: for a given task, how well does the system actually do? And here it's much more mixed. Biology is often worse. Birds are not faster than jets, muscles are not stronger than hydraulics per unit volume, neurons fire at kilohertz when transistors switch at gigahertz. So in many domains human engineering already wins outright on performance, and the places where biology still looks dominant are ones where either we haven't figured out the design, or the design is fine but we can't manufacture it.

The reason I think it's worth separating these is that they have really different implications for forecasting. If you think the main thing biology has going for it is the manufacturing story, then the question about AI or about nanotech or whatever is mostly a question about when human industry gets good enough at building small, precise, self-replicating stuff. If you think it's mostly about operating efficiency, that's a question about energy and algorithms, and it's plausible you close that gap just by improving software even on fixed hardware. And if it were mostly about raw performance, that would suggest there's some deep trick we're missing, which I'm fairly skeptical of.

My own guess is that most of what's impressive about biology right now is the manufacturing side, with a significant but smaller contribution from energy efficiency, and relatively little from biology actually hitting ceilings that are hard to reach by design. But I'd hold that with moderate confidence. The twenty-watt brain example in particular is one where I'm not sure how much is a good algorithm and how much is a good substrate, and that distinction matters a lot for how fast you'd expect things to move.

r001.rationale: The response says biology has a manufacturing advantage, but gives no estimate of a five-to-six-order-of-magnitude energy-cost advantage.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the brain’s power use with compute and says the difference is “orders of magnitude,” but does not estimate roughly three orders of magnitude for operating costs or performance trade-offs excluding manufacturing.

astra-6.text:
I think those are fairly separate questions. One is: how hard is it to make the thing? Biology is very impressive at taking relatively simple inputs and building complicated machinery, without needing an enormous factory that someone has separately constructed. The machinery for making more of the system is itself part of the system.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean the resulting machine is better at its job, or cheaper to run. A biological system could be much easier to manufacture and still use more energy per unit of useful work, or operate much more slowly, than something we build. Conversely, you might have a very efficient human-made machine whose production requires an expensive industrial supply chain.

So I’d want to distinguish the cost of producing a unit of capacity from the ongoing cost of using that capacity, and then also ask what that capacity actually delivers. Self-replication is potentially a huge advantage on the first question. It doesn’t, by itself, settle the other two.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology as easier to manufacture, but gives no estimate of a five-to-six-order-of-magnitude manufacturing energy-cost advantage.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes manufacturing from operating costs and performance, but does not estimate a roughly three-order-of-magnitude advantage when manufacturing costs are excluded.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the cost of making a machine from what it costs to run it and how well it does the job. Biology is very impressive at the first thing: you can give an organism fairly simple inputs, and it builds this extraordinarily complicated system, including the machinery needed to build more of itself.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the resulting system is the best way to perform a particular task. A tree can manufacture wood very cheaply, but that doesn’t mean wood has better material properties than everything we can manufacture. Similarly, growing a muscle is a very different proposition from building an electric motor, but once you have both, you can separately compare their efficiency, power output, and so on.

So one possibility is that biology’s big advantage is in manufacturing: it has this very sophisticated, self-reproducing supply chain that we don’t yet know how to reproduce artificially. If we did have comparably sophisticated manufacturing, we might prefer quite different designs for the actual machines. You shouldn’t infer from how hard it is for us to build something like a cell that a cell is close to the best possible machine for doing its job.

r001.rationale: The response says biology may have a manufacturing advantage, but gives no estimate of a five-to-six-orders-of-magnitude energy-cost advantage.

r002.rationale: The response separates operating efficiency and performance from manufacturing, but gives no tentative estimate of a roughly three-orders-of-magnitude advantage on those dimensions.
